w02.002: The Finite Story, Chapter I, The Creative Thesis of Perfection (pp. 31–37)
w02.003: The second universe age, which Sadler names "the Finite Story," opens with the creation of the Seven Master Spirits and the Ancients of Days and closes when the evolution of the Supreme Being is complete. It did not begin abruptly. The twilight of the first age shaded slowly into the dawn of the second. In this period Deity begins to work on the "creative level" and, through the association called God the Sevenfold, reaches out into time and space. Eternal Havona, meanwhile, becomes the "thesis of perfection" set before the imperfect universes that surround it.
w02.005: Having treated in his prologue an eternity without beginning or end, Sadler now shifts the scene. The second major division of his book, "The Finite Story," is built from three chapters: the creative thesis of perfection, the evolutionary antithesis, and the first synthesis, God the Supreme.
w02.006: Most of The Urantia Book is in fact the story of the evolving seven superuniverses, the story of what is taking place here and now. Creation and evolution in time and space finally find their destiny in superuniverses perfected under the sovereignty of the Supreme Being; that, in brief, is the plot of the second universe age.
w02.007: Sadler stresses that, unlike the eternity before it, this is an age we can "understand." The second age has a beginning and an end in time. For a reader who has been groping through past eternity, this brings the relief of solid ground underfoot. Sadler even suggests that the real study of the master universe begins at this point.
w02.008: The Framework of Thesis, Antithesis, and Synthesis
w02.009: Sadler reads the history of the master universe as a repeating pattern of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. Something perfect is given first (thesis); something imperfect appears over against it (antithesis); and as the imperfect grows into perfection, the two are bound into one (synthesis). The framework is not The Urantia Book's own language; it is an interpretive tool Sadler has borrowed. Yet because the text treats the perfection of Havona and the imperfection of the evolving universes as complementary partners, and presents the Supreme Being as their synthesis, the scheme meshes well with the movement of the revelation.
w02.010: 2. The Dawn of Time: The Opening of the Second Age (orig. pp. 32–33)
w02.012: What brought the Havona age to a close and opened the age of the superuniverses? Sadler's answer is that no single moment did so. Just as the sky lightens little by little before sunrise, the twilight of the first age passed gradually into the dawn of the second. The events described below are those that took place, one after another, in that transition.
w02.013: Sadler first sets one conjecture in parentheses. Long before the second age formally began, he supposes, the Architects of the Master Universe may have sent force organizers out into the superuniverse space level to gather energies and organize nebulae. The text gives no such chronology; this is Sadler's inference.
w02.014: The Seven Master Spirits: The First Experiential Deity
w02.015: Sadler regards the first event after eternity, that is, after Havona, as the appearance of the Seven Master Spirits. Though these exalted spirits are not absolute beings, they stand for Paradise Deity on all levels short of the absolute. In Sadler's terms these are the finite, the subabsolute, and the finite-subabsolute levels; in more familiar words, the supreme, the ultimate, and the supreme-ultimate.
w02.016: Sadler draws out two essential points about the Master Spirits. First, they are experiential rather than existential beings, the first expression of experiential Deity. Second, each of them personally embodies one of the seven ways in which the three Deity persons can be combined: Father, Son, and Spirit singly; the paired Father-Son, Father-Spirit, and Son-Spirit; and the threefold Father-Son-Spirit.
w02.018: Here Sadler makes an intriguing connection. Because there are mathematically only seven ways to combine three persons, there are seven Master Spirits, and for that very reason the space level of the superuniverses came to be divided into seven segments. The Urantia Book clearly pairs the seven superuniverses with the Seven Master Spirits, but the causal claim that the number of segments "derives" from the number of combinations is Sadler's interpretation.
w02.019: God the Supreme Appears in Havona
w02.020: At some point in that twilight another event took place: God the Supreme made his appearance in Havona. His presence had its source in the Paradise Trinity, and he existed as a spirit person. He was present in the central universe even before the superuniverses were formally organized. Yet then, as now, creatures could not approach him or make direct contact with him.
w02.022: God the Supreme began as a spirit person without power. How power comes to be added to that spirit person is the central thread of Chapters 6 and 7.
w02.023: The Trinity's Mandate and the Ancients of Days
w02.024: Next, under the mandate of the Paradise Trinity, the grand universe is organized: Havona is placed at the center, with the seven superuniverses arranged around it. Sadler thinks that about this time the Trinity created the twenty-one Ancients of Days who would govern the seven superuniverses in groups of three. Soon afterward the seven superuniverse capitals were constructed, and the Ancients of Days would then have left Paradise to take up residence on their capital spheres.
w02.026: Creator Sons, Creative Spirits, and Mortals
w02.027: Somewhat later the Father and the Son begin to create the Creator Sons, and the Infinite Spirit responds by bringing forth the Creative Spirits as their complements. In due course these Universe Sons and Universe Spirits are commissioned as rulers of local universes, and the second age comes into full flower. Before long evolutionary mortals appear on the worlds of space, and the pilgrims of time set out on the long ascent to Paradise in search of the Universal Father.
w02.028: From the twilight of the first age to the dawn of the second: events on the grand universe side and on the Havona side (dashed box: Sadler's conjecture)
w02.030: Sadler lingers over this transition in order to show what the newly appearing beings have in common. From mortal man up to the Master Spirits and God the Supreme, the new beings of the second age are all experiential. They do not know everything before they have experienced it; they grow by learning and living.
w02.031: The creators are no exception. Creator Sons and Creative Spirits change in status as they pass through the experience of organizing and perfecting their local universes. If existential Deity is the One who "already is all," experiential beings are beings who are "becoming." The second age is the age of becoming.
w02.032: 3. God the Sevenfold: Creative Deity (orig. pp. 33–36)
w02.033: A Living Ladder Between God and Man
w02.034: With the organization of the seven superuniverses, the creative association known as God the Sevenfold began to function. Sadler presents God the Sevenfold as the creative and associative extension of the Paradise Deities outward into time and space. This is how Deity makes contact with every creature of the superuniverses and local universes. Figuratively, it is a living ladder made of divine personalities, spanning the gap between a human being and the Paradise Father.
w02.036: This association functions on seven levels, and its members fall into three broad groups. At the top are the familiar Paradise Deities: the Universal Father, the Eternal Son, and the Infinite Spirit. In the middle is the experiential Deity, the Supreme Being. Below are the Supreme Creators, made up of the Creator Sons, the Ancients of Days, and the Seven Master Spirits.
w02.037: The seven levels and three groups of God the Sevenfold. Mortals climb this ladder from the Creator Son at the bottom
w02.038: What is new is the corps of Supreme Creators, the "post-Havona creators." They organize and perfect the seven superuniverses and the seven hundred thousand local universes still to come. Each Master Spirit pervades one superuniverse and determines its individual character; the Ancients of Days rule each superuniverse as a triad; and each Creator Son, together with a Creative Spirit, creates or evolves a local universe and its native life.
w02.039: Which Way to Count the Seven Levels
w02.040: The Foreword of The Urantia Book counts the levels of God the Sevenfold from the bottom up: number 1 is the Paradise Creator Sons and number 7 is God the Father [0:8.2–8]. This follows the order in which an ascending mortal actually meets them. In this chapter Sadler counts the other way, putting the Father first, but in the summary chart of the next chapter he again places the Creator Son first. Whichever end we begin from, the content is the same. Counted from the top, the ladder shows the path by which Deity descends; counted from the bottom, it shows the path by which a person ascends.
w02.041: The Supreme Being holds a unique place in this association. Sadler calls him the evolving experiential Deity and explains that his gradual emergence rests on three things: what the Supreme Creators achieve in the realms of time and space, the fruit of their successful cooperation with the Paradise Deities, and the Supreme Being's own striving to grow.
w02.043: Sadler pauses here to observe that Deity has entered a new level of activity. The Foreword tells us that total Deity functions on seven levels [0:1.3]. In his prologue Sadler took Deity to have begun on the static level, passed through the potential level, and by the dawn of the first age to have been working on the associative level. Now a fundamental difference between the first and second ages comes into view: Deity has entered the fourth level of activity, the creative.
w02.045: What does this mean? As Sadler explains it, Deity has now begun to draw upon the vast reservoir of potential reality, the potentials of the three Absolutes. Basic potentials that are prespirit, premind, and prematerial are transmuted and begin to emerge in the new universes as fresh spirit, fresh mind, and fresh matter.
w02.046: The process of creation is, in effect, a process of transmutation. Whether it be a new spirit personality, a new functional level of mind, or a new nebula that will one day become the material of a local universe, these "new realities," Sadler explains, come ultimately from the three Absolutes of potentiality. To extend the image of the reservoir: until the first age it had only been filling, and in the second age the sluice gates opened for the first time, letting water flow out across the fields.
w02.047: 4. Second-Age Havona: The Thesis of Perfection (orig. pp. 36–37)
w02.048: A Precreation Universe and a Pattern Universe
w02.049: In the prologue Sadler treated first-age Havona as precreative, as something that in fact never had a beginning. Strictly speaking, that is probably the right way to classify the central universe. Yet in practical terms, in relation to the superuniverses, Havona is a creation, the pattern universe of divine perfection.
w02.050: In the second age Havona becomes the divine thesis of perfection, a challenge from God set before the imperfect evolving universes that surround it. To every creature God extends this invitation:
w02.052: Sadler holds that this mandate is addressed not only to individual creatures but also to every Creator Son and Creative Spirit. Can they, through experiential creation and evolution, reproduce in their own domains the everlasting perfection of the existential universe that lies at the heart of all things? Havona is the model; the evolving universes are the workshop in which that model must be studied and the same work fashioned anew.
w02.054: Sadler does not see this relationship as running only one way. If Havona challenges the imperfect superuniverses, those needy superuniverses in turn challenge Havona. The central creation answers long before the first mortal ascender reaches its settled realms. Coming events cast their shadows ahead.
w02.055: As the first age enters its "twilight," challenge enters changeless Havona for the first time. New beings appear. Havona's seven circuits have always existed, yet Circuit Spirits are now found at work in each of them. Power centers take up permanent stations in the seven circuits. Every one of the billion spheres receives its Universe Censors. Thus the central creation makes ready for the events to come.
w02.057: When Grandfanda, the first mortal pilgrim, reaches Havona, a host of new developments follows. A new order of ministering spirits, the secondary supernaphim, appears. Citizens of Paradise begin an outward pilgrimage through Havona. The first Graduate Guide welcomes Grandfanda.
w02.059: Ascenders from the superuniverses bring the seeds of evolutionary growth into the central creation. So the Havona of the second age remains an eternal, precreative universe while also becoming a creative and changing, even an evolving, universe. When guests entered the perfect house, the house itself began to change in order to receive them.
w02.060: The second universe age, "the Finite Story," begins with the creation of the Seven Master Spirits and the Ancients of Days and ends when the evolution of the Supreme Being is complete. It is an age we can understand, with a beginning and an end.
w02.061: The passage from the first age to the second was not a sudden event but a gradual process, like twilight turning to dawn.
w02.062: The Seven Master Spirits are the first experiential Deity and express the seven combinations possible among the three persons of Deity. Sadler finds in this number the reason there are seven superuniverses.
w02.063: Before the superuniverses were organized, God the Supreme was present in Havona as a spirit person but functioned only on spiritual levels.
w02.064: God the Sevenfold is a ladder composed of three groups, the Paradise Deities, the Supreme Being, and the Supreme Creators, and it shows that Deity has entered the creative level.
w02.065: The new beings of the second age, creators included, are all experiential; they learn and grow.
w02.066: In the second age Havona becomes the "thesis of perfection," and at the same time, challenged by the superuniverses, a changing universe that welcomes new beings such as the Circuit Spirits and the Graduate Guides.
w02.067: The Evolutionary Antithesis: The Challenge of Imperfection
w02.068: The Finite Story, Chapter II, The Evolutionary Antithesis (pp. 38–47)
w02.069: If the perfection of Havona is the thesis, the seven superuniverses, which began imperfect, form the vast antithesis set against it. Sadler reads this imperfection not as a defect but as an empty space in which growth is possible. God the Sevenfold is Deity's response to that challenge, and the Supreme Being evolves by taking in the power that streams from the achievements of the Supreme Creators. In the latter part of the chapter Sadler brings cosmology down to the level of personal life and asks how a human being answers God's challenge here and now.
w02.072: In the present universe age the divine central universe is clearly the creative thesis of perfection. The superuniverses, which started out imperfect, are the vast antithesis to Havona's perfection. Sadler says that these imperfect universes became the greatest challenge to the Paradise and Havona personalities who serve as creators and administrators of the evolutionary realms. Taking eternal and divine perfection out into realms that are by nature imperfect and evolving is what Sadler calls the first great adventure, the "Supreme Adventure."
w02.073: In The Urantia Book the subject of the "supreme adventure" is usually the creature seeking God.
w02.075: Sadler turns the phrase around and sees the venture of eternal beings into an imperfect world as an adventure as well.
w02.076: A God Who Delights in Adventure
w02.077: Sadler states plainly that this study puts forward a particular view: that God possesses qualities of being that are "ancestral" to the joy of adventure seen in the character of progressing creatures, to their tendency to respond to the stimulus of a challenge. Otherwise, why would He suddenly have set before the Paradise-Havona system of eternal perfection the astonishing challenge of the profound imperfection of the seven superuniverses?
w02.078: In the first universe age everything was in balance; neither disharmony nor disorder had ever been known. Then God extends this creation outward into space. The universe now comes to include realms not yet physically settled, realms where imperfect creatures will appear, realms where even evil and sin may arise through their unwise choices. How must beings who had known only harmony have reacted when they first saw disorder, and first watched potential evil become actual evil through the choices of creatures? Sadler invites the reader to pause and imagine it.
w02.079: The Gift of the Power of Choice
w02.080: Each creature of this new creation received from God the priceless power of choice. In Sadler's phrase, each creature is a sovereign within itself. It decides for itself whether to become a citizen of the universe, whether to become a son of God, and no one can intrude upon that choice, because the One who gave the power is God. Without this gift of personality we would be nothing more than living machines. Because of this (relative) free will we can choose to become ascending sons of God, or we can go on choosing wrongly.
w02.081: Sadler marvels at God's daring here. To unite the purest spirit with mortal man, the lowest creature able to receive personality, and to seek eternal partnership with children of animal-origin races: only a God who combines the spirit of adventure with divine love could undertake such a thing.
w02.082: 2. God the Sevenfold: Evolving Deity (orig. pp. 40–42)
w02.084: God the Sevenfold is Deity's response to the challenge of imperfection. At the same time, by way of the bestowals of the Paradise Sons as creatures, God the Sevenfold brings a counterchallenge, divine perfection itself, into the innermost core of the evolving domains, to the inhabited worlds themselves.
w02.085: In this chapter Sadler reorganizes God the Sevenfold from the standpoint of function: three groups interacting within the seven levels, namely the Supreme Creators, the Supreme Being, and the triune Paradise Deity. The cooperating beings of these three groups work in time and space across the potential, associative, creative, and evolutional levels. And through their successes in the evolving universes the Supreme Being is slowly evolving as experiential Deity.
w02.087: In the previous chapter Deity entered the fourth level, the creative. Now Sadler finds Deity at work on the fifth level, the evolutional.
w02.089: The Supreme Being is evolving. At the dawn of the second age he begins as a spirit person in Havona. Then, each time the Supreme Creators succeed in perfecting the imperfect creation, worlds like our own included, he grows and evolves.
w02.091: Sadler compares this process to a river. The successes of the Supreme Creators and of their coordinates, associates, and subordinates are like countless springs and rivulets. These gather into brooks, the brooks into larger streams, and the streams into the tributaries of a great river. This "great river" of divine achievement in time and space is what The Urantia Book calls the experiential power of the Almighty Supreme.
w02.093: As a river flows into the sea, this gathering almighty power is united with the Supreme's spirit person in Havona. Here lies the source of the growing sovereign power of the Supreme. Having begun as a spirit personality entirely without sovereign power, the Supreme gradually grows into the experiential sovereign of the seven superuniverses.
w02.094: The Difference Between Creation and Evolution: Time
w02.095: The Supreme Creators themselves, and especially the Creator Sons and Creative Spirits, also evolve. Sadler sums up the difference between creation and evolution in a single word: time. Creation happens in an instant; evolution slows the process of transmutation so that creatures can understand what is happening and take conscious part in their own growth. It is the difference between being handed a photograph and painting a picture together.
w02.097: The Supreme Being does not merely receive these efforts passively. According to Sadler, he reaches into the creative and associative levels to bring the potentials of the Paradise Deities into actuality, and by identifying himself with every growing creature he gradually brings himself into actuality.
w02.098: 3. The Emptiness of Imperfection: The Capacity for Growth (orig. pp. 42–43)
w02.100: Born into the second age, we take evolutionary growth and finite experience for granted, but seen from a wider perspective this belongs uniquely to our own universe age, the age in which the Supreme is growing. He grows because we grow, and we can grow because we grow within him. Sadler asks us to picture the grand universe as the stage on which the Supreme Being evolves. Our growth takes place within him, and his within us; the process runs both ways.
w02.102: Other ages will have experience too, but it will be postfinite or superfinite experience. When the growth of the Supreme is finished and he emerges as a Deity whom all of us can know, the opportunity to share in that growth, the possibility of finite experience itself, will also come to an end. This is why Sadler prizes the present age.
w02.103: The Privilege of Starting from the Lowest Place
w02.104: Human beings begin on the lowest rung of finite creature life. Beginning as little more than animals, they are given the chance to rise by evolutionary growth all the way to the high status of the finaliter. Sadler expresses this as a paradox: because we begin lowest, our opportunity is greatest; because we begin with least, we can hold the most.
w02.105: Here Sadler draws on Lao-tzu's Tao Te Ching and its teaching that a vessel is useful because it is empty. Just as the virtue of a vessel lies in its capacity to be filled, the virtue of imperfection lies in its capacity to be filled with the experience of growing consciously toward perfection. It is precisely the imperfection of the time-space creation that makes such growth possible. Had the superuniverses been created perfect from the start, they would have been merely an extension of the central creation, another Havona on a larger scale.
w02.107: This empty space is an opportunity for those who have come down from above as well. The very needs of the superuniverses, their lack of perfection, open new opportunities of growth to the Paradise-Havona personalities. They themselves grow in the enlarged service of helping us attain the heights of divine perfection from which they descended.
w02.108: 4. The Challenge of Unifying Power and Personality (orig. pp. 43–44)
w02.110: It is the Supreme who sets the second age's pattern of growth. As the almighty sovereign now emerging over the superuniverses, he draws power from what the Supreme Creators do and achieve, and from the deeds of everyone who lives in the universes of time and space. When their deeds are evil, his growth is impeded; when they are good, his growth is enlarged.
w02.112: How the Supreme grows in time and space hinges on the inflow of almighty power. And this gathering power is united with the Supreme's spirit person in Havona through the action of the mind bestowed on the Supreme Being. The Urantia Book even names the place.
w02.114: The point Sadler emphasizes can be put in one sentence: through the unifying action of mind, power becomes one with spirit personality and comes under its control. Sadler calls this principle of growth the "power-personality synthesis" and says that we will meet it again and again throughout The Urantia Book.
w02.116: The power-personality synthesis: almighty power gathering from below, spirit personality coming from above, and Supreme Mind added from the side meet on the pilot world of the outer Havona circuit
w02.118: According to Sadler, in the time-space universes energy-matter starts first and is dominant, while spirit is still striving for dominance. Spirit alone is powerless; mind is needed to master matter. And only personal mind can master energy-matter and still choose to submit to spirit. Mind that refuses the leading of spirit will not, in the end, endure for long.
w02.119: Sadler takes the present world as his example. We have mastered many of nature's forces and secrets, and we are frightened. Recalling the nuclear weapons of the Cold War years in which the book was written gives the remark even greater weight.
w02.120: Why the Meek Inherit the Earth
w02.121: To the question "How can the meek inherit the earth?" Sadler answers that only the meek can inherit the earth and keep that inheritance. Such a meek person, of course, must first be strong. When the strong are meek, their strength frightens no one; when they are not meek, they breed fear, and that fear eventually calls forth a greater counterforce, an alliance of the fearful, which brings them down.
w02.123: So Sadler sums up the growth challenge of the present age this way: can we master the physical creation by mind and then, by the choice of personality, place that victorious mind under the control of spirit? If we can, we become people who are both strong and meek. The power-personality synthesis of the Supreme Being is repeated in miniature in an individual life.
w02.126: In the last section of the chapter Sadler turns from cosmology to personal spirituality. His starting point is what The Urantia Book says about the keys of the kingdom of heaven.
w02.128: Sadler reads this teaching as placing a high value first on honesty and then on courage, the moral strength of character. Exercising moral courage and making moral decisions builds moral strength. Where, then, is that strength directed? If it turns inward toward the self, everything is lost; at best it remains on the ethical level. But if it turns inward toward the spirit nucleus of the person, the Adjuster, everything is gained. Morality then reaches out toward the spiritual and goes beyond ethics.
w02.129: From Humility and Hunger to Mercy and Ministry
w02.130: The search for God begins with a hunger of the human heart, and that hunger springs from the humility of recognizing one's own smallness. Sadler calls this, which happens when a strong person weighs the human will against the will of God, the triumph of meekness over pride.
w02.131: At this point Sadler pictures a person's growth toward maturity as a kind of chain. When humility, hunger, and meekness are added to moral strength, there grows a relative wisdom and the generous maturity that Sadler calls an "anticynical sophistication." The wise, childlike faith of such a person is entirely different from the blind presumption of an ignorant and childish faith.
w02.132: This insight produces not sentimentality but a tender heart that responds in practice to the needs of others. Since the capacity to feel need is the same as the capacity to feel pain, a tender heart is open to hurt. In time tenderness, humility, and insight melt together and blossom into a rich humor. When we are aware at once of God's infinity and our own smallness, a humor grows that is turned against the ever-hungry self, and those who can laugh at themselves learn to live at peace with themselves.
w02.133: A person in whom humor and wisdom have been fused with sympathy and understanding can comfort others effectively, and in comforting develops the capacity to accept the same ministry of understanding and to benefit from it. Sadler says that such kindly and mature understanding becomes the foundation of true mercy. The Urantia Book teaches that mercy is not something simple but a quality of growth that develops by stages.
w02.135: Mercy is love in action, but love made wise and discerning by the insight of experience. And mercy actually applied is ministry.
w02.138: The chain of response to challenge: the process of maturing that begins with sincerity and decision and arrives at mercy and ministry (Sadler's outline)
w02.139: Sadler adds that the effectiveness of ministry depends not only on the unselfishness of the love but also on the wisdom it contains. Clumsy giving may leave a spiritual benefit to the giver, yet do nothing at all for the one being helped. Truly constructive giving calls for wisdom, humor, experience, and love working together, and the person who gives in this way becomes, in Sadler's phrase, one who is "waging peace."
w02.140: The Beatitudes and the Here and Now
w02.141: Such a person is not afraid to live on earth as a citizen conscious of the universe. Sadler adds a proviso, however: so strong an inner assurance is safe only when it is bound to sincerity and humility and when the self is held in check by a living sense of humor.
w02.142: This, Sadler surmises, is why Jesus spoke the beatitudes to the twelve apostles. The happiness of the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the persecuted overlaps with the chain of maturity traced above. Sadler quotes the Gospel of Matthew, but The Urantia Book presents the same scene as the ordination sermon [140:3].
w02.144: For Sadler, God's challenge is not something remote or theoretical but the most practical thing one can know in this life. The challenge, the response, and the growth that results are all "here and now." The challenge of the God who inhabits eternity lies always in the ever-present "now," and we answer it not with regrets about the past or resolutions about the future but with the decisions and actions we take now.
w02.145: A Challenge Fitted to Each Person
w02.146: The Universal Father has generously supplied what we need to answer this challenge: the power of choice that comes with personality, and the Adjuster, our spirit nucleus and guide to Paradise. Having so endowed us, He challenges us greatly and watches patiently to see what we will do.
w02.148: God asks everything of each person, but that "everything" is always proportioned to the capacity to give. Sadler recalls the scene by the sea in which the risen Jesus asked John and Peter, "Do you love me?", asked Andrew, "Do you trust me?", and asked Thomas, "Will you serve me?" [192:2]. The challenge is always fitted to the individual.
w02.150: In the end the question Sadler leaves us with is simple. God has enriched us and challenges us to use our "talents" so that they yield a return for ourselves and for His creation. Above all, though, He challenges us with an infinite love so intense it could blind us. To this love, which we can feel even where we cannot understand, how will we respond here and now?
w02.152: The Urantia Book paragraph numbers Sadler attaches in this section do not always fit the content exactly. The reference 5:6.1, placed at the end of the paragraph about God equipping and challenging us, concerns the Father as the bestower of every personality. In 28:6.2 the subject of "take note of the man, in what manner he was born" is the Conjoint Actor. Such citations are better read as threads for reflection than as literal proof texts.
w02.153: If Havona's perfection is the thesis, the seven superuniverses that began in imperfection are the antithesis. Sadler calls the bearing of eternal perfection into imperfect realms the "Supreme Adventure."
w02.154: Sadler advances the view that God possesses an adventurous quality that responds to challenge. The power of choice given to creatures lies at the heart of this adventure.
w02.155: In the second age Deity functions on the fifth level, the evolutional. The Supreme Being begins as a spirit person and grows by receiving almighty power gathered from the successes of the Supreme Creators.
w02.156: The difference between creation and evolution is time. Evolution allows creatures to take conscious part in their own growth.
w02.157: Imperfection is not a defect but an emptiness that can be filled. The opportunity to grow through finite experience exists only now, in the age of the growth of the Supreme.
w02.158: The power-personality synthesis is the principle by which power comes under the control of spirit personality through mind; in personal life it appears as a character that is both strong and meek.
w02.159: God's challenge comes here and now, fitted to each person's capacity and need, and we answer it with decisions and actions.
w02.160: The First Synthesis: God the Supreme
w02.161: The Finite Story, Chapter III, First Synthesis: God the Supreme (pp. 48–55)
w02.162: As the second age ends, light and life is established throughout the seven superuniverses, and the Supreme Being emerges to rule the perfected superuniverses experientially. Sadler sees this as the first synthesis, binding together the perfection of Havona (thesis) and the perfected superuniverses (antithesis). He finds the same kind of synthesis in the trinitization of finaliters with Havona natives, in the convergence of the cultures of the seven superuniverses, and in the partnership of Creator Son and Creative Spirit. Much of the latter half of the chapter is Sadler's reasoning about a future that has not been revealed.
w02.163: 1. A Quiet Time Between Ages (orig. pp. 48–49)
w02.165: In this chapter Sadler's study moves into the future of time. He therefore promises to speak of the events of each chapter's own period in the present tense, of earlier chapters in the past, and of later chapters in the future. This commentary generally follows the same practice.
w02.166: The Assumption of a Quiet Time
w02.167: Just as there is a "quiet zone" between adjacent space levels, Sadler assumes there may also be a "quiet time" between universe ages. The Urantia Book does not say this directly; it is Sadler's analogy, reasoning from the structure of space to the structure of time. The assumption allows him to consider, on its own, the complete achievement of evolutionary destiny as the second age ends, without having to deal at the same time with the events bound up in the opening phase of the next age.
w02.168: In that quiet time the grand universe enjoys completed growth, the satisfaction of destiny attained. The long, hard labor of evolution has at last won its experiential victory. The Supreme Creators have answered Havona's challenge of perfection; the outcome is seven hundred thousand perfected local universes, crowned by the establishment of light and life in all seven superuniverses.
w02.169: Sadler likens the time-space creation of this period to a boat that has shipped its oars and rests. During the quiet time the grand universe becomes, like the Havona of the first age, a self-contained creation: enjoying satisfaction instead of toil, consolidating what it has achieved, and completing its unification under the sovereignty of the newly emerged Supreme Being.
w02.170: 2. The Emergence of the Supreme Being (orig. pp. 49–50)
w02.171: A God Who Can Be Approached
w02.172: What carries the second age to the summit of finite growth is the Supreme Being's last emergence, as experiential ruler over the perfected superuniverses. A Deity hitherto unapproachable becomes a Deity whom every creature can contact. God the Father, being infinite, will always remain a mystery, but God the Supreme, being finite, can be understood by finite creatures. Because all finite creatures have evolved together within him, that experiential kinship becomes the basis of mutual understanding.
w02.174: The Supreme Level: From Going Out to Gathering In
w02.175: Here Sadler comes to the sixth level on which total Deity functions, the supreme level. He arranges the levels into three groups. The static, potential, and associative levels are precreative, the levels on which Deity prepared for the adventure of going out into time and space. The creative and evolutional levels are levels of "going out," on which Deity distributes Himself throughout the creation and identifies Himself with creatures through the indwelling of the Adjusters. Their activity is seen most clearly in the ministry of God the Sevenfold.
w02.177: Now, on the sixth level, Sadler sees a "coming in." What was poured out across the whole creation is gathered back again. The Supreme represents the first great synthesis, the union of the thesis of perfection with the antithesis of imperfection; and the antithesis here is imperfection that has attained perfected status through evolutionary growth. On this level even Deity is experiential. As the nature of the Paradise bestowal Sons shows, on this level God and man can become one.
w02.178: How Sadler reads the seven levels of total Deity: precreative, going out, gathering in, and the next story
w02.179: An image from breathing makes this easier to grasp. If Deity drew breath up to the first age and, throughout the second, breathed out as it were, giving Himself to the whole creation, then the supreme level is the moment of breathing in again. Yet the breath drawn in is not the same as the breath let out: it now carries the experience of countless creatures.
w02.180: 3. A Synthesis at the Creature Level (orig. p. 51)
w02.181: The Union of the Perfect and the Perfected
w02.182: Events of the far future are hard to picture, but Sadler shows that the same type of synthesis is already occurring among certain creatures. Havona supplies the original thesis, perfection; the imperfection of the superuniverses is the antithesis; and this imperfection can become perfect through evolutionary growth. Is there, then, a synthesis of the perfected and the perfect at the level of creatures?
w02.183: Sadler offers the trinitizing union of finaliters with Havona natives as an example.
w02.185: Sadler invites us to imagine a scene. Could any being be farther from a Havona native than an unwashed cave dweller on a primitive planet? Yet such a one, indwelt by an Adjuster, may survive, be received into the Corps of the Finality, and then, as a finaliter, join a Havona native in the adventure of trinitization. It is, quite literally, a synthesis of the perfected and the perfect.
w02.187: Even so, a difference remains between eternal perfection and perfection won through experience. In Sadler's witty contrast, the Havona native assumes that things have always worked well, while the ascender knows that things work well because we have learned the laws, and that once they did not work well at all. The one takes it for granted; the other is grateful.
w02.188: 4. The Completed Grand Universe: Divergence and Convergence (orig. pp. 50–52)
w02.189: The Seven Natures of the Seven Master Spirits
w02.190: Throughout the second age each superuniverse developed separately under the distinctive influence of one Master Spirit. Because the Seven Master Spirits personalize the seven possible combinations of the three Deities, each differs in nature. Sadler symbolizes this with three overlapping circles: three regions that do not overlap, three where two circles overlap, and one where all three overlap, seven regions in all.
w02.191: The Seven Master Spirits and the seven combinations of Deity (the seven regions of the three-circle figure)
w02.199: Center where all three circles overlap
w02.200: Master Spirit Number Seven, who presides over Orvonton, the seventh superuniverse to which we belong, is a balanced union of the characteristics of the three Deities [34:2.6]. This is the source of The Urantia Book's expectation that Orvonton, though slower to develop than the other superuniverses, will in the end become a well-balanced creation.
w02.202: Each Master Spirit pervades and dominates the whole environment of one superuniverse. Each superuniverse and its native beings are therefore distinctive as well, forever bearing the individual nature and character of the Master Spirit who oversees them. Sadler expects each superuniverse to tend toward its own culture, its own "civilization."
w02.203: When the Supreme Being emerges as sovereign of all the superuniverses, the barriers that have separated the supercreations are lifted, and for the first time the seven superuniverses function as one administrative and cultural whole. Sadler foresees that the blending of seven cultures will give new stimulus to growth, and he calls this the principle of "divergence and convergence." Growth first becomes distinctive through divergence; then, when the time is ripe, what has developed in isolation is brought together and consolidated into one.
w02.204: Sadler notes that this parallels the development of an ordinary inhabited world. The evolutionary races first separate and cultivate their own cultures, and later blend into one through the Adamic peoples and the Edenic civilization. To borrow an image from the orchestra: after a long season in which seven instruments rehearse separately, the day finally comes when they play one piece together.
w02.205: 5. The Creative Unions of Dual Deity (orig. pp. 52–53)
w02.206: The Central Partnership of Each Age
w02.207: Beyond divergence and convergence, Sadler identifies one more principle: in a given universe age, some particular creative union of dual Deity appears to have special importance.
w02.208: In the first age the significant dual-Deity union was that of Father and Son. The union of the Father and the Son trinitized the Infinite Spirit and eternalized the perfect central universe. In the second age the dual-Deity union that matters most appears to be the partnership of the Son and the Spirit. The Urantia Book describes the relationship this way.
w02.210: Sadler judges, however, that this active partnership of Son and Spirit seems to be carried out less on Paradise than in the local universes, in the joint work of Creator Son and Creative Spirit. They are the ones who create, organize, and perfect the evolutionary realms. A question therefore arises. If the outcome of the Father-Son union was the appearance of the Infinite Spirit and of Havona, what will be the final outcome when the seven hundred thousand Son-Spirit partnerships in time and space are complete?
w02.212: Sadler sets the unions of the two ages side by side. The union of Father and Son is existential in kind, an eternal event on Paradise. The unions of Son and Spirit are experiential in kind, temporal events out in space. Sadler does not think that on Paradise itself the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit form any new partnership. Rather, the Son and the Spirit of Paradise are in partnership through the persons of their Universe Sons and Universe Spirits.
w02.213: Sadler then reasons one step further. Once light and life has been established in every local universe, he proposes, the seven hundred thousand Universe Sons and Universe Spirits may enter into trinitizing unions. Because not until the second age draws to its very end do the local universes attain a status comparable (in a finite way) to the perfection of the central creation, he expects the counterpart of the trinitization that opened the first age to occur only then. This is a bold conjecture of Sadler's with no basis in The Urantia Book.
w02.214: The dual-Deity unions of the two ages. The outcome at lower right is Sadler's conjecture about something not revealed
w02.215: 6. Son and Spirit in the Second Age (orig. pp. 53–55)
w02.216: The Evolution of the Creator Son: Growing as a Person
w02.217: Looking back to the Zero Age, the Eternal Son was fully personal even before Havona. Sadler holds that the same is true of a Creator Son. A Creator Son is wholly personal even before his local universe has begun, and long before it is settled in light and life. The whole of Michael's evolutionary growth, including his experience and training before he became a creator, therefore takes place as a personal being.
w02.218: The sevenfold Creator Son, the Master Michael, is experientially far greater than he was at his first appearance on Paradise, newly born of the Universal Father and the Eternal Son. He has experienced much in organizing and perfecting his local universe, and through his seven bestowals in the likeness of creatures he has added to his nature much that his original Paradise endowment of divinity did not contain.
w02.219: Sadler reads this through the framework of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. The Master Michael still personalizes the "thesis" of original divinity conceived jointly by the Father and the Son, while adding an experiential nature, the "antithesis," drawn from the imperfection of the time-space creation. Just as Jesus of Nazareth still lives in Michael of Nebadon, the nature of the creature is present in his nature. By personally synthesizing these opposing qualities, Sadler suggests, the Master Michael comes to resemble and express the experiential divinity of the Supreme Being.
w02.221: The Evolution of the Creative Spirit: Attaining Personality
w02.222: Sadler sees the Creative Spirit growing along a different path. In the Zero Age the Infinite Spirit was not yet a person, and attained personality status by functioning as cocreator in the actualization of Havona; that is the interpretation Sadler established in his prologue. He holds that the Creative Spirit attains personality status in the same way, by working as cocreator in perfecting a local universe.
w02.223: Sadler's comparison runs like this. As the Infinite Spirit attained personality status as an event of eternity, simultaneous with the appearance of Havona, so the Creative Spirit attains personality status as an event of time, when her local universe is settled in light and life. A creative being comes to resemble the universe it makes, and attains personality status in the course of making it. If so, the early experience of a Creative Spirit would be that of a prepersonal being, very different from the growth of a Creator Son, who is a person from the beginning.
w02.224: The Six Phases of the Creative Spirit in The Urantia Book
w02.225: This passage of Sadler's needs to be read alongside the text. The Urantia Book outlines the career of the local universe Mother Spirit in six phases [17:6.2]: initial Paradise differentiation, preliminary creatorship training, the stage of physical creation, life creation, the postbestowal ages, and the ages of light and life. Yet already in the fourth phase there is a "personalization" ceremony on Paradise [17:6.7]; the Creative Spirit bestows mind only after receiving personal prerogatives [34:4.8]; and in the fifth phase she is elevated to cosovereignty [17:6.8]. Sadler's statement that she attains personality status only when the universe is settled in light and life therefore does not match the text as it stands. He probably had in mind the full experiential achievement of personality.
w02.227: Sadler says that this sixth phase appears to be the present limit of a Creative Spirit's growth. A Spirit matured in this way is experientially very different from her first-phase counterpart, who had only just been differentiated in the Infinite Spirit when her future partner, the Creator Son, was born. In sum, a Universe Son, as he grows, joins to his native Paradise divinity the experiential nature of time-space creatures. A Universe Spirit, as she grows, gains the experience of attaining personality in time: what was first focalized as a new Creative Spirit, a distinct presence of the Infinite Spirit, becomes personal.
w02.228: Two paths of growth for Universe Son and Universe Spirit in the second age (Sadler's outline)
w02.230: The Eternal Son, a person even before Havona
The Infinite Spirit, who attained personality with Havona (Sadler's interpretation)
w02.231: A focalization within the Infinite Spirit
w02.232: Adds creature nature through experience (seven bestowals)
w02.233: The sixth phase (ages of light and life)
w02.234: Because the two kinds of growth are so different, they complement each other all the better. Sadler believes that, taken together, they would encompass all the growth a creative being can achieve in the second universe age.
w02.235: The Son-Spirit Union and the Associate Creator
w02.236: Not since the Father and the Son joined to trinitize the Conjoint Actor have any two creators brought forth a third being equal to themselves in creative nature and creator attributes. Sadler thinks the trinitizing union of a Universe Son and a Universe Spirit must wait until the second age is nearly over, or perhaps until the third begins. It will not happen, he holds, until all seven hundred thousand local universes are settled in light and life.
w02.237: When such a union takes place, the dual-Deity union is transformed into a triune relationship: two become three. Sadler calls the coordinate third being who would arise in this way the "Associate Creator" and names the threefold union the "Son-Spirit Creative Trio." According to Sadler, this Associate Creator would express five things:
w02.238: the original Paradise divinity received by the Creator Son and the Creative Spirit
w02.239: the experience of the Universe Son and Universe Spirit in organizing and perfecting a local universe
w02.240: the experiential creature nature the Creator Son gained in the course of his seven bestowals
w02.241: the experiential personality status the Creative Spirit gained in time as a cooperating creator
w02.242: the "superadditive" result of the union of Creator Son and Creative Spirit
w02.243: For the wording of the last item, Sadler borrows The Urantia Book's description of the personality of the Infinite Spirit.
w02.245: Sadler also suggests that such a third being, like the Infinite Spirit, might be subordinate in sovereignty yet the most versatile in action. This, too, is language The Urantia Book originally uses of the Infinite Spirit.
w02.247: Sadler predicts that this Associate Creator might reveal a supreme-ultimate nature, and that the Son-Spirit Creative Trios will play an important role in opening the Primary Space Level and developing the universes of outer space. The symmetry is this: as the Infinite Spirit, born of the Father-Son union, became the partner of all creation after Havona, so the third being of the Son-Spirit union would become the partner in the creation of outer space. It is a beautiful symmetry, but The Urantia Book has never revealed such a being. It is a conjecture Sadler lays down as a bridge into the story of the subabsolute.
w02.248: As the second age ends, light and life is established in all seven hundred thousand local universes and all seven superuniverses, and Sadler assumes a "quiet time" between the ages.
w02.249: The Supreme Being emerges to rule the perfected superuniverses experientially and, being finite, becomes a God whom finite creatures can approach and understand.
w02.250: Sadler reads the levels of total Deity as precreative (static, potential, associative), going out (creative, evolutional), and gathering in (supreme).
w02.251: The trinitization of finaliters with Havona natives is an example, at the creature level, of the synthesis of the perfected with the perfect.
w02.252: Superuniverse cultures that grew separately under the seven natures of the Seven Master Spirits are brought together under the sovereignty of the Supreme. This is the principle of divergence and convergence.
w02.253: If the central partnership of the first age was Father-Son, that of the second age is Son-Spirit, realized through the Creator Sons and Creative Spirits of the local universes.
w02.254: The Creator Son grows as a person by adding creature nature; the Creative Spirit grows by achieving experiential personality in time. Sadler's account of when the Creative Spirit attains personality should be read alongside the text.
w02.255: The Son-Spirit Creative Trio and the Associate Creator are Sadler's conjectures about an unrevealed future.
w03.002: The Absonite Story, Chapter IV “Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Universes” (pp. 57–61)
w03.003: Having finished the Finite Story, Sadler opens the second large division of his book, the Absonite Story, and brings in a fresh interpretive tool: the master universe pictured as a living, growing organism. Just as a cell has a nucleus and the cytoplasm around it, so the master universe is said to have a central nucleus wrapped in a surrounding cytoplasm. Using four criteria to identify a nucleus, Sadler names Havona the first nuclear universe and the completed grand universe the second. The four outer space levels, he concludes, do not form a third nucleus; together they make up a single body of cytoplasm.
w03.005: Sadler gives the second story of his book the name “The Absonite Story.” Its subject is twofold: the evolution of the outer space universes, and the continuing growth of the grand universe until, under the sovereignty of God the Ultimate, it is at last joined with those outer creations into one. Of the six chapters that make up this story in the original, the first three are treated here in Chapters 8 to 10 and the last three in Chapters 11 to 13. The story opens with the first entry into the Primary Space Level and closes when God the Ultimate at last emerges in full. Where the Finite Story covered a single age, this one spans four.
w03.006: 2. The Cell as Analogy: Nucleus and Cytoplasm (orig. p. 58)
w03.007: Why borrow the language of biology
w03.008: At this point Sadler introduces a pair of terms, nucleus and cytoplasm. Should the master universe be regarded as one great organism in the process of growing, then at its center there should be a nucleus, and around that nucleus a cytoplasm.
w03.009: In a cell, the nucleus is the organ that directs growth and reproduction and hands on hereditary characteristics; the cytoplasm is everything in the cell apart from the nucleus. Sadler illustrates with an egg: the yolk corresponds to the nucleus, the white to the cytoplasm. The nucleus is small, yet it carries the inheritance at the center; the cytoplasm is extensive, yet it grows by receiving what the nucleus imparts.
w03.011: Sadler’s proposal is that the master universe has two nuclei. One is Havona, the existential nucleus. The other is the grand universe, Havona together with the seven superuniverses, which forms an existential-experiential nucleus.
w03.014: Sadler begins by removing the Isle of Paradise from consideration as a nucleus, since Paradise belongs to no universe, the master universe included. The Havona space level, by contrast, ranks first among the space levels of the master universe, and the Havona age opens the sequence of universe ages. On these grounds Sadler takes Havona to be the grand universe’s nucleus.
w03.016: What would entitle a given universe to be called a nucleus? Sadler sets out four criteria, and they carry the argument of the whole chapter.
w03.017: The first is a **unique nature**. Havona differs from the superuniverses at the level of its very nature. Its origin is eternal and its perfection existential. The superuniverses, by contrast, had their origin in time; they start out imperfect, move slowly toward perfection by evolution, and will finally be perfect in the experiential sense.
w03.018: The second is the **appearance of Deity**. The appearance of eternal Havona is bound up with the appearance of a new Deity, the Infinite Spirit. The Urantia Book reports this simultaneity on the Spirit’s own testimony.
w03.020: The third is the **formation of a Trinity**. The appearance of the Infinite Spirit opened the way for the three Deities to join together as the Paradise Trinity. The emergence of Havona, the emergence of the third Deity, and the forming of the Trinity all coincide in a single “moment.”
w03.021: The fourth is **transmission**. A nucleus passes its characteristics outward. In Havona’s case the hereditary trait of divine perfection reaches the outlying superuniverses, the cytoplasm, through the creators and administrators of Paradise-Havona origin who serve in the creations of time and space. Sadler points to the ministry of the Supreme Creators as a clear instance.
w03.022: Measured by these four marks, Havona seems quite plainly to be the nucleus of the grand universe. Is it, then, the nucleus of the whole master universe as well? Sadler answers no. Because the completed grand universe will set in motion a sequence of events resembling the one that accompanied the appearance of Havona, it is the grand universe that serves as the nucleus of the master creation.
w03.023: 4. The Second Nucleus: The Completed Grand Universe (orig. pp. 59–60)
w03.025: Sadler names the grand universe the “Second Nuclear Universe.” To test the claim, newly appeared Havona must be compared with the grand universe in its *completed* state, that is, once light and life has settled over all seven superuniverses and the Supreme Being has emerged as a Deity with whom contact can be fully made.
w03.027: As to nature, the completed grand universe is fundamentally unlike the universes of outer space. It is the spatial arena in which the Supreme Being finishes His experiential growth, and so no other region of the master universe can resemble it. Every creation that comes afterward is post-Supreme and lacks finite experience.
w03.028: As to the appearance of Deity, the completion of the grand universe is linked with the emergence of a new Deity, the Supreme Being. As to the Trinity, the final emergence of the Supreme makes possible the first experiential Trinity. Its membership joins the Supreme Being with two corps, the Master Architects and the Supreme Creators; since the Supreme cannot function in it before He has fully emerged, its factual formation must also wait for the grand universe to be completed. The Urantia Book makes the same point.
w03.030: As to transmission, the hereditary trait of the grand universe is “finite experience.” It is carried to the cytoplasmic universes of outer space through the Supreme Being, through the first experiential Trinity, and through the multitude of finaliters and other beings who will serve in those realms.
w03.031: Four marks of a nucleus (as Sadler arranges them)
w03.033: The only arena in which the Supreme grew
No basic difference from the other outer levels
w03.036: Merely extends the level before it
w03.037: Sadler’s conclusion, then, is twofold: Havona is the first nuclear universe, lying at the heart of the grand universe; and that larger whole is in turn the second nuclear universe, lying at the heart of the master universe. In terms of the egg, it is as if a germ lay within the yolk, and the whole yolk were in turn enclosed by the white.
w03.038: 5. Outer Space as One Cytoplasm (orig. pp. 60–61)
w03.040: A natural question follows. With Havona as first nucleus and the grand universe as second, will the Primary Space Level, once fully grown, join with the grand universe to form a third and larger nucleus? Again Sadler answers no, and he tests the answer against the same four marks.
w03.041: As to nature, the four outer space levels do not differ from one another in the way Havona differs from every later creation, or the grand universe from the outer universes. The universes on all four levels are post-Supreme universes, organized after the Supreme Being has fully emerged. The authors of The Urantia Book likewise observe that these universes have no share in the Supreme’s evolution.
w03.043: The other marks give the same result. No new Deity appears when the Primary Space Level is completed. Without a new experiential Deity there can be no new experiential Trinity. And with neither a new Deity nor a new Trinity to carry a trait outward, each succeeding level appears simply to extend and enlarge the one before it. The Secondary and Tertiary Space Levels yield the same verdict.
w03.044: Sadler accordingly proposes that the four outer space levels form one cytoplasmic unit whose nucleus is the grand universe.
w03.045: The cellular structure of the master universe as Sadler pictures it: Havona the first nucleus, the completed grand universe the second, and the four outer space levels a single cytoplasm
w03.046: The Urantia Book also uses the word “nucleus,” though not quite as Sadler does.
w03.048: Sadler and the text: how “nucleus” is used
w03.049: The Urantia Book calls Paradise the “⟦Q 14:0.1⟧gigantic nuclear Isle of absolute stability⟦/Q⟧” [14:0.1] and, as quoted above, speaks of the Paradise-Havona System as a whole as the nucleus of the master universe. In the text, “nucleus” refers to the center of spatial arrangement and of gravity. In Sadler, following the biological analogy, it refers to a center of growth that hands on its characteristics. Leaving Paradise out of the nucleus, and calling the completed grand universe the nucleus of the master universe, are definitions made within that analogy. They are best read not as a challenge to the text but as a different emphasis placed on the same word.
w03.050: The Absonite Story concerns the evolution of the outer space universes and the eventual union of the grand universe with them under the sovereignty of God the Ultimate; it spans four universe ages.
w03.051: Sadler likens the master universe to a growing organism and introduces the terms nucleus and cytoplasm.
w03.052: A nuclear universe is recognized by four marks: a unique nature, the appearance of Deity, the formation of a Trinity, and the transmission of a trait.
w03.053: Havona’s appearance coincided with that of the Infinite Spirit and with the Paradise Trinity, and it transmits divine perfection; it is the first nuclear universe.
w03.054: The completed grand universe is linked with the Supreme Being’s emergence and with the first experiential Trinity, and it transmits finite experience; it is the second nuclear universe.
w03.055: The four outer space levels give rise to no new Deity and no new Trinity, so they do not become a third nucleus; they are a single cytoplasm around the grand universe as nucleus.
w03.056: The Urantia Book calls the Paradise-Havona System the nucleus of the master universe; Sadler’s “nucleus” is a figurative definition with a different focus.
w03.058: The Absonite Story, Chapter V “The Transformation of Synthesis” (pp. 62–65)
w03.059: In this brief chapter Sadler weaves together the cycle of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis and the distinction between nucleus and cytoplasm. Havona, the superuniverses, and the completed grand universe make up the first cycle, but a synthesis that has reached its destiny does not come to rest; it turns into a new thesis. The emergence of a new Deity personalizes the old synthesis, and the formation of a new Trinity presents the new thesis. Sadler offers this “transformation of synthesis” as a basic principle running through the entire growth of the master universe, and on that basis he looks ahead to the second cycle.
w03.061: The first thesis: when did Havona become a nucleus?
w03.062: Laying the thesis-antithesis-synthesis pattern of the Prologue over the nucleus-cytoplasm pattern of the previous chapter gives the first cycle a new reading. Havona began as a pre-creative existence and later became the thesis of divine perfection. Sadler asks: when did Havona become a nucleus? At what point did it stop being a creation that existed in and for itself? At what point did it turn into a challenge?
w03.063: His answer is: when the Deity union of God the Sevenfold came into being, that is, when this union began to function as the superuniverses were being organized. A nucleus cannot be a nucleus by itself; it needs a surrounding cytoplasm. Likewise a challenge requires a challenged party. For God the Sevenfold to act as the challenge of divine perfection, there had to be something present to receive that challenge.
w03.064: The first antithesis: the counter-challenge of the cytoplasmic superuniverses
w03.065: The native imperfection of the superuniverses is the antithesis to perfect Havona, and the seven superuniverses stand as cytoplasm to Havona as nucleus. Their imperfection becomes a counter-challenge, the challenge of need. It meets God the Sevenfold and every personality of the Paradise-Havona system who has come down into the time-space universes to help imperfect creatures rise to the heights of evolutionary perfection.
w03.066: In a parenthesis Sadler adds a short and kindly remark. As the perfection of God is a challenge to each of us to ascend, so our imperfection is a challenge of service to beings who are divinely perfect. Challenge does not run in one direction only.
w03.067: The first synthesis: a union demonstrated on three levels
w03.068: The completed grand universe is a synthesis of the perfect and the perfected. Sadler finds this synthesis demonstrated on three levels. On the creature level it appears when a human being fuses with the indwelling Adjuster and finds God on Paradise. On the creator level it appears when God takes on human nature, as the Paradise Sons do in their bestowals. On the Deity level it appears in the final emergence of the Supreme Being through the power-personality synthesis of all finite reality.
w03.069: Man ascends, God descends, and the sum of their meeting is personalized as one Deity. This is the first cycle, the subject of the Finite Story.
w03.070: 2. The Synthesis Becomes a New Thesis (orig. pp. 63–64)
w03.071: What follows the attainment of destiny
w03.072: When thesis and antithesis arrive at synthesis, things that were at first so unlike, and that challenged each other, are joined as one. That is the attainment of destiny, or at least of the destiny implicit in the original challenges of thesis to antithesis and of antithesis to thesis.
w03.073: Yet in Sadler’s view the attainment of destiny always sets something new in motion. If the only result of settling the superuniverses in light and life and completing the grand universe were the emergence of the Supreme Being, then at the end of the present age the grand universe might enter a static condition in which it no longer grew. But the appearance of the Supreme sets off further events. As a direct result of His full growth, the first experiential Trinity takes form as a factual reality. The Urantia Book makes this sequence plain.
w03.075: A new Deity for the old synthesis, a new Trinity for the new thesis
w03.076: Here Sadler sets down the central proposition of the chapter. The completion of the Supreme Being expresses and rounds off the completion of the first synthesis, and the first experiential Trinity, once formed, is the event that turns this first synthesis into the second thesis. If the completed Supreme corresponds to “destiny attained,” the coming into being of the new experiential Trinity, the Ultimate Trinity, corresponds to the “new challenge” put forth by a new thesis. That new challenge sets a larger and higher destiny ahead.
w03.077: Sadler then raises this to a general principle: the old synthesis becomes the new thesis; the old synthesis is personalized by the appearance of a new Deity, and the new thesis is presented by the formation of a new Trinity. He holds that this “transformation of synthesis” is a basic principle running through the entire growth history of the master universe.
w03.078: A mountain offers a comparison. The moment of standing on the first summit is a completion, yet only from there does a higher summit come into view. Because the first experiential Trinity has the whole master universe, and not the grand universe alone, as its field, it is a genuinely new thesis: the second thesis.
w03.079: The words of the text and Sadler’s framework
w03.080: That the Ultimate Trinity comes into full function after the Supreme Being is completed, and that its goal is the integration of the master creation, is what the text itself states [106:3.2, 106:4.2]. To gather this into the principle that “synthesis is transformed into thesis,” and to treat it as a law repeated in every universe age, is Sadler’s interpretation; the text gives the principle no name. What can be confirmed from the text is the observation that the pairing “appearance of a Deity, followed by formation of a Trinity” occurs both in the first age (the Infinite Spirit, then the Paradise Trinity) and in the coming third age (the Supreme Being, then the Ultimate Trinity).
w03.081: 3. Looking Ahead to the Second Cycle (orig. pp. 64–65)
w03.082: The second thesis: the grand universe as base
w03.083: With the principle that synthesis becomes new thesis in hand, Sadler looks ahead to what will follow once the second thesis appears on the spatial stage of the master universe. The grand universe must first be reassessed. As the first synthesis, it has reached its destiny; as the new nucleus, it stands at the threshold of a larger and newer destiny. As the second nuclear universe, the grand universe becomes the base of power for the second thesis, the first experiential Trinity, as it reaches outward. From this nuclear base the Trinity and the countless personalities it will mobilize will work their way outward into the cytoplasmic creations on all four outer space levels.
w03.085: The second antithesis must belong to the realm of the outer space levels. The outer universes will differ from the grand universe as much as the superuniverses differed from Havona. Being post-Supreme in nature, they are wholly incapable of finite experience.
w03.086: The second synthesis: still far off
w03.087: If this reasoning about the second thesis and the second antithesis is correct, their mutual challenge must logically issue at last in a second synthesis: the union of the outer universes as cytoplasm with the inner creations as nucleus. But such a synthesis is possible only when the entire master universe has grown up and finished its final development. Sadler promises to show in later chapters how vast an undertaking that is. The Urantia Book foresees the outcome of that completion in these words.
w03.089: Two cycles linked by the transformation of synthesis: the first synthesis (the grand universe and the Supreme Being) turns into the second thesis (the Ultimate Trinity), which faces outer space
w03.091: Seen from a great height, the master universe appears to develop rather rapidly. After the first cycle come the second thesis and the second antithesis, and these will open a second great adventure in outer space, at present uninhabited. Following the “Supreme Adventure” of the second age, Sadler calls this one the “Ultimate Adventure.”
w03.092: Sadler weaves together the thesis-antithesis-synthesis cycle and the nucleus-cytoplasm distinction.
w03.093: Havona became both nucleus and thesis only when God the Sevenfold began to function, that is, when there were cytoplasmic superuniverses around it.
w03.094: The imperfection of the superuniverses is a counter-challenge of need addressed to divine perfection; challenge comes from both sides.
w03.095: The first synthesis is demonstrated on three levels: creature (Adjuster fusion), creator (the bestowals of the Sons), and Deity (the emergence of the Supreme Being).
w03.096: A synthesis that reaches destiny does not stand still. A new Deity personalizes the old synthesis, and a new Trinity presents the new thesis; Sadler calls this the basic principle of the “transformation of synthesis.”
w03.097: In the second cycle the thesis is the first experiential Trinity based in the grand universe, the antithesis is the outer space levels, and the synthesis is the completion of the whole master universe.
w03.099: The Absonite Story, Chapter VI “The Second Creative Thesis” (pp. 66–74)
w03.100: The emergence of the Supreme Being brings at least four new factors onto the absonite level: the first experiential Trinity, the Supreme Being acting both within and beyond it, the Corps of Supreme Creators, and the post-finite creatures who took part in the Supreme’s growth. At the center stands the Ultimate Trinity. More than 1.4 million personalities are involved, yet it is a union of three Deity realities, an experiential Trinity that grows and learns. Sadler portrays this Trinity setting out from the grand universe as its base toward outer space, in a scene of mobilization and great migration.
w03.101: 1. One Hour and Ten Thousand Years (orig. p. 66)
w03.102: Sadler says that the Absonite Story truly begins in this chapter, and he conveys its length through a comparison. Were the entire Finite Story to take roughly an hour to tell, telling the whole Absonite Story would take more than ten thousand years. The figure is meant to convey the difference in scale rather than to serve as an exact calculation; its basis is examined separately in an appendix.
w03.103: 2. Four Factors on the Absonite Level (orig. pp. 66–68)
w03.104: The Finite Story closed with the seven superuniverses brought to perfection and the Supreme Being emerging as their experiential sovereign. Once God the Supreme steps onto the stage of universe action, a number of changes take place on the absonite level of existence. Sadler identifies at least four new factors.
w03.105: The first experiential Trinity and the Supreme Being
w03.106: The first factor is the first experiential Trinity, the Ultimate Trinity, of which the Supreme Being is a member alongside the Corps of Supreme Creators and the Master Architects. The second factor is the Supreme Being Himself. While functioning as the Deity member of this Trinity, the Supreme also acts personally in the master universe. Sadler sees this as His activity as a “super-almighty” and as the expression of new and as yet unknown potentials of mind.
w03.107: The Corps of Supreme Creators: two aspects
w03.108: The third factor, the Corps of Supreme Creators, calls for a double view. Taken as one unified Deity, the Corps belongs to the Ultimate Trinity. Yet every individual Supreme Creator also acts in person throughout the post-Supreme master universe. Its members (Creator Sons and their partner Creative Spirits, the Ancients of Days, and the Seven Master Spirits) were the creative leaders of the Paradise-Havona personalities who, at the dawn of the second age, set out on the “Supreme Adventure” into the imperfect superuniverses. They have completed that adventure, and in evolving along with their domains their own status and nature have changed.
w03.109: Sadler illustrates with a comparison between a Creator Son and a Master Son. Both belong to the same order. A Creator Son embodies the essence of Paradise divinity, whereas a Master Son has added to his nature the experience of organizing a local universe and earning sovereignty through seven bestowals in the likeness of his own creatures. Michael of Nebadon is such a Son. His composite nature has absorbed the natures of Melchizedek, Lanonandek, Adam, and seraphim, together with three levels of human nature: spiritual, morontial, and material. The Urantia Book lists the traces of these bestowals as follows.
w03.111: The text goes on to say that this experience links Michael with the Ultimate Trinity.
w03.113: There will be seven hundred thousand beings like Michael. Sadler goes further and conjectures that the younger Creator Sons and Creative Spirits who did not receive a local universe in the second age may assist their seniors in outer space and form a “Second Corps of Supreme Creators.” This conjecture is not in the text. On the other hand, the text does look ahead directly to the capacity of these creators to function beyond the finite.
w03.116: The fourth factor consists of the perfect and perfected personalities who took part in the Supreme’s growth. Joined with the Supreme, they move beyond their former limits and embark on a fresh adventure, seeking, on a new level of ultimate reality, the goal toward which creature existence moves. Among them are the mortal finaliters, their fellows in the six finaliter corps of non-mortal origin, and numerous associates who are not finaliters. While serving in the universes of outer space, they will also take up the absonite quest for God as the Ultimate.
w03.117: These four factors will carry into the outer universes the “finite experience” distilled in perfecting the seven superuniverses, and so will deeply shape their development.
w03.120: Sadler pairs two events: the Supreme Being’s emergence personalizes, as Deity, the first great synthesis, while the first experiential Trinity, in taking factual form, gives Deity expression to the second great thesis. The members of this Trinity are three: the Deity of the Corps of Master Architects, the Deity of the Corps of Supreme Creators, and the Deity of the Supreme Being. The Foreword of The Urantia Book states the same composition.
w03.122: When only three are involved, as with the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, it is easy to think of a Trinity as something like a loose partnership. In the Ultimate Trinity, Sadler points out, so many personalities are involved that such a view becomes impossible. Counting the Creative Spirits who are paired with the Creator Sons, the personalities connected with this Trinity number no fewer than 1,428,040.
w03.123: The three Deity realities that make up the Ultimate Trinity and the number of personalities involved (breakdown reconstructed by the commentator)
w03.124: How is that figure reached? Sadler does not give a breakdown here, but the numbers in the text account for it exactly. The Master Architects total 28,011 [31:9.10]. On the side of the Supreme Creators there are seven Master Spirits, twenty-one Ancients of Days, 700,000 Creator Sons, and 700,000 Creative Spirits, for 1,400,028. Adding the one Supreme Being gives precisely 1,428,040.
w03.125: The point of the figure is clear. A Trinity is an actual reality existing quite apart from the personal beings associated with it. Each of the 1.4 million personalities may enter into personal relationship with the factual reality of the Ultimate Trinity, yet the Trinity is a union they form not as persons but as Deity. A choir offers a comparison: the music comes from the voice of every singer, yet the chorus is a single reality that belongs to no one singer.
w03.126: The three members one by one
w03.127: **The Deity of the Corps of Master Architects.** These universe planners already existed in the first age, and perhaps in the Zero Age as well. They are absonite beings who personalize God’s plan for the master creation; in Sadler’s phrase, they are “living blueprints.” They have planned the whole master universe, from Havona out to the Quartan Space Level, and they have co-ordinated the master creation until the Ultimate Trinity becomes factual. Their membership in this Trinity is not individual but that of the unified Deity of the whole Corps.
w03.128: **The Deity of the Corps of Supreme Creators.** Here Sadler draws a striking analogy. What the completed evolution of the Almighty Supreme means to the Corps of Supreme Creators, he suggests, parallels what the Infinite Spirit’s appearance meant for the Father-Son partnership. The power of the Almighty grows out of the success of the Supreme Creators, and Sadler reasons that this very success binds their whole experiential divinity into one Deity reality. No single one of these more than a million personalities can be a member, but the unified Deity of the Corps can. That Deity reality would combine the original perfection of Paradise divinity with qualities gained by living, striving, and overcoming in time and space.
